title: System Design Course — APIs, Databases, Caching, CDNs, Load Balancing & Production Infra
description: A structured path through Hayk Simonyan’s freeCodeCamp course on designing production systems: starting from a single server, then databases, scaling, load balancing, API styles, and finally authentication, authorization, and security. Watch each chapter in the original YouTube video, then use the summary, quiz, and exercise to lock in the idea.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.summary: Hayk Simonyan opens by saying that moving from a mid-level developer to a senior engineer means shifting focus from simply writing code to high-level architecture. He previews the path: foundations, API design (including REST, GraphQL, and gRPC), databases, caching, CDNs and load balancing, large-scale data, designing for production, and how he approaches system design interviews.

quiz.question: According to the opening, what focus shift is required to move toward senior engineering work?
choices: From simply writing code to high-level architectural design
From architecture to only writing CSS
From interviews to never drawing a diagram
From HTTP to only using FTP
quiz.explanation: Hayk opens by saying that transitioning from a mid-level developer to a senior engineer requires shifting focus from simply writing code to mastering high-level design.

quiz.question: Who developed this freeCodeCamp course?
choices: Beau Carnes
Keerti Purswani
Hayk Simonyan
Quincy Larson
quiz.explanation: The official description and freeCodeCamp article credit Hayk Simonyan (@hayk.simonyan).

exercise.prompt: Write three questions you would ask before designing a production system (for example about users, scale, or what must not fail).
exercise.hint: Good starting questions include who the users are, expected traffic, latency or availability targets, and which data must stay correct.

lessons.content:
## From writing code to designing systems

Hayk Simonyan opens this longer system-design course with a career shift, not a product diagram. Moving from mid-level development toward senior engineering work means changing what you spend your attention on. It is no longer enough to write features that pass tests. You also have to think about **high-level architecture**: how services talk, where data lives, how the system fails, and how it will grow.

This course is his walk through those foundations. The written lessons that follow are meant to stand on their own, so you can learn the same ideas without sitting through the video first. The optional “Watch this part” section at the bottom of each lesson still links to the freeCodeCamp upload if you want Hayk’s delivery.

## What the course covers

Hayk previews a path you will meet again, in this order:

- **Foundations** — starting from a single server, then databases, scaling, load balancing, health checks, and single points of failure.
- **API design** — including the three styles he keeps returning to: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC, plus the application and transport protocols underneath them.
- **Security of those APIs** — authentication (who is calling), authorization (what they may do), and a set of concrete protection techniques.
- Later pillars he names for further study: databases in more depth, caching, CDNs, load balancing at scale, large-scale data, designing for production, and how he approaches **system design interviews**.

The point of the preview is orientation. You do not need every later topic in the first ten minutes, but you should know that API design sits in a larger production picture.

## How to use these notes

Each lesson in this course is a full written version of one video segment. Read the explanation, study the diagrams and tables, then use the quiz and exercise to check that the written content stuck. Watch the corresponding clip only if you want the lecture itself.

## Common pitfalls

- Treating “senior” as a title instead of a change in what you design for: scale, failure, and contracts with other teams.
- Jumping straight to a trendy API style (GraphQL, gRPC) without first being able to draw a single-server baseline.
- Watching the intro as a trailer and skipping the later security lessons; those later chapters are part of the same course promise.

## Key takeaways

- Senior-oriented work shifts attention from “just writing code” to high-level architectural design.
- This course, developed by Hayk Simonyan and published on freeCodeCamp, starts with foundations, then APIs (REST, GraphQL, gRPC), then authentication, authorization, and API security.
- The later production topics he names — databases, caching, CDNs, load balancing, large-scale data, and interview practice — are the context those APIs live in.
- You can learn each segment from the written lesson; the video is optional.

lessons.title: Single server setup
lessons.summary: Designing for millions of users is hard, so the course starts with the simplest picture: one server. A domain name is resolved through DNS to that machine’s IP, and clients send HTTP requests to it. This baseline makes later chapters — adding a database, more servers, and a load balancer — easier to motivate.

quiz.question: In a basic single-server web setup, what does DNS typically do?
choices: Store the application’s user table
Map a domain name to the server’s IP address
Balance traffic across many regions automatically
Compile the server’s source code
quiz.explanation: Clients look up the hostname, then connect to the address they receive.

quiz.question: Why start a system design with a single server?
choices: Because one server is always enough in production
It is a clear baseline; you add databases, replicas, and load balancers as bottlenecks appear
Because DNS cannot work with more than one host
Because HTTP only supports a single machine
quiz.explanation: The course builds from a simple setup toward production concerns rather than starting with every possible component.

exercise.prompt: Sketch a single-server path: user types a URL, DNS returns an IP, the browser sends an HTTP request, the server returns a response. Label each step.
exercise.hint: Browser → DNS lookup → IP → HTTP request to the one server → HTML or JSON response.

lessons.content:
## Start with the simplest picture

Designing for millions of users is hard if you start there. Hayk begins with a **single-server** web setup so later chapters — adding a database, more servers, and a load balancer — have a clear baseline to grow from.

In this picture there is one machine that both serves the application and, at first, may even hold the data. A user types a **domain name**. **DNS** maps that name to the server’s **IP address**. The client then sends an **HTTP** request to that IP, the server runs the application code, and it returns a response.

```text
Browser  --DNS-->  domain → IP
Browser  --HTTP-->  one server (app + maybe data)
```

That is the entire system on day one of many products. It is easy to reason about: there is one place to deploy, one place to look when something is slow, and one place that can fail.

## Why this baseline matters

A single server is not the destination. It is the starting point you *deliberately outgrow*. As traffic grows you will notice bottlenecks:

- The machine runs out of CPU, RAM, or disk.
- The application and the data fight for the same resources.
- A restart or a hardware fault takes the whole site down, because there is no second instance.

Those pressures are what justify a separate database, then more app servers, then a load balancer in front of them. If you skip the single-server drawing, it is harder to explain *why* each of those pieces appeared.

## What DNS and HTTP are doing here

Two ideas from this segment are worth locking in:

- **DNS** is not the website. It is the lookup that turns a human-readable name into an address the client can connect to.
- **HTTP** is the application-level request/response the browser (or another client) sends once it has that address. Later lessons will add TLS, APIs, and other protocols, but the baseline conversation is still “client asks, one server answers.”

## Common pitfalls

- Drawing a load balancer on the first version of a design when there is only one server behind it; that is ceremony, not a requirement yet.
- Forgetting DNS when explaining how a user reaches the box.
- Treating a single server as “not real architecture.” It is real architecture — just the smallest useful one.

## Key takeaways

- Start a system design with one server so later additions have a reason.
- DNS maps a domain name to the server’s IP; clients then send HTTP requests to that machine.
- You add databases, extra servers, and load balancers as bottlenecks and failure modes appear, not because the first drawing looked too simple.

lessons.title: Databases: SQL, NoSQL, and graph
lessons.summary: As the user base grows, a single server is no longer enough to store and serve all of the data, so you need a database that matches the access pattern. SQL (relational) databases fit structured records and transactions. NoSQL covers models such as documents, key-value, and wide columns. Graph databases are built for highly connected data. The point is to choose the model for the problem, not to treat one type as universal.

quiz.question: When is a relational SQL database usually a strong default?
choices: Only for storing video files as blobs and nothing else
When you have structured records and need transactional, relational queries
When the only operation is a key lookup with no relationships
When you must store only graph edges
quiz.explanation: Tables, schemas, and ACID-style transactions are the usual reason to start with SQL.

quiz.question: What is a graph database particularly well suited to?
choices: Highly connected data, where relationships are a first-class part of the query
Replacing DNS
Serving only static CSS
Guaranteeing UDP delivery
quiz.explanation: Social graphs, recommendations, and similar problems often map cleanly onto graph stores.

exercise.prompt: For each of these, pick SQL, a document/key-value NoSQL store, or a graph database and say why: bank transfers, a flexible product catalog, and 'friends of friends' recommendations.
exercise.hint: Transfers lean SQL (transactions). A catalog often fits documents. Friend-of-friend queries often fit a graph.

lessons.content:
## When one machine cannot hold all the data

As the user base grows, a single server is no longer enough to store and serve all of the data. You introduce a **database** chosen for the access pattern, not because one type is fashionable.

Hayk’s point in this segment is selection: match the data model to the problem.

## Relational (SQL) databases

**Relational** databases store records in tables with a defined schema. Rows can be related with keys, and the database is typically strong at **transactions** — a group of writes that should all succeed or all fail together.

A SQL database is usually a strong default when:

- The data is structured and the relationships matter (users, orders, payments).
- You need transactional guarantees and ad hoc relational queries.
- Many parts of the product will query the same consistent model.

## NoSQL and graph models

**NoSQL** is a family of non-relational stores, not a single product. Common shapes include:

- **Document** databases, which store JSON-like documents and fit flexible or evolving records.
- **Key-value** stores, which look up a value by a key and are often used for caches and simple records.
- **Wide-column** stores, which organize data for large, sparse, or write-heavy workloads.

**Graph** databases are called out separately because they treat **relationships as a first-class part of the query**. They are a good fit for highly connected data — social graphs, recommendation “who knows whom,” fraud rings — where walking edges is the main workload, not just storing a blob.

The lesson’s advice is consistent with the earlier concepts course, but the emphasis here is practical: do not treat one database type as universal. A document store that is perfect for a content catalog may be a poor home for money movement that needs multi-row transactions. A graph database is not a substitute for a payment ledger.

```text
App servers
     |
     +-- relational DB   (structured, transactional)
     +-- document / KV   (flexible or simple lookups)
     +-- graph DB        (highly connected queries)
```

## Common pitfalls

- Picking NoSQL only because “it scales,” then rediscovering you needed transactions.
- Putting highly connected queries into tables and hoping joins stay cheap forever, when a graph model would have matched the access pattern.
- Keeping the database on the same single server after it has already become the bottleneck.

## Key takeaways

- Introduce a database when one server can no longer store and serve the data well.
- SQL (relational) databases fit structured records and transactional, relational queries.
- NoSQL covers documents, key-value, and wide-column models; graph databases are built for highly connected data.
- Choose the model for the access pattern; no one type is universal.

lessons.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
lessons.summary: The lesson contrasts the two primary scaling approaches. Vertical scaling means giving one machine more CPU, memory, or disk — simple until you hit the limits or cost of a single box. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines and spreading work across them, which adds capacity but also coordination: you need a way to route traffic and, often, to split or replicate data.

quiz.question: What is vertical scaling?
choices: Adding more machines and splitting work across them
Giving a single machine more resources, such as CPU, RAM, or disk
Deleting unused regions
Turning off the load balancer
quiz.explanation: You scale 'up' the existing box. Horizontal scaling is scaling 'out' to more boxes.

quiz.question: What is a typical trade-off of horizontal scaling compared with vertical scaling?
choices: It is always simpler and never needs routing changes
It can add more capacity, but you must distribute work and often change how data is stored or routed
It only works for front-end static files
It removes the need for any database
quiz.explanation: More machines mean load balancing, and often sharding or replication, not just a larger instance type.

exercise.prompt: A web app’s single server is CPU-bound at peak. List one vertical step you might try first and one horizontal step you would take if that is no longer enough.
exercise.hint: Vertical: a larger instance. Horizontal: more app servers behind a load balancer.

lessons.content:
## Two ways to add capacity

Once you have an application and a database, growth forces a scaling choice. Hayk contrasts the two primary approaches.

**Vertical scaling** (scale *up*) means giving a *single* machine more resources: a faster or additional CPU, more RAM, more or faster disk, a better network link. You keep the same mental model — one box — and you make that box stronger.

**Horizontal scaling** (scale *out*) means adding *more* machines and spreading work across them. Capacity grows with the size of the pool, but you must now **distribute work** and, often, change how data is stored or routed: replication, sharding, or a load balancer in front of identical app servers.

| Approach | What you add | Typical upside | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical | CPU, RAM, disk, or network on one machine | Simple operations; no new coordination | A hard ceiling; bigger boxes get expensive; one machine is still one failure |
| Horizontal | More machines | Capacity can grow past one box; you can survive a node loss | You must route traffic and often split or copy data |

## How the trade-off shows up in a design

Vertical scaling is the first, honest move when a single server is “almost enough.” Many products live here longer than architecture diagrams suggest. The limit is real, though: there is a largest instance you can buy, and when that machine is down, so is the service.

Horizontal scaling is what later lessons are preparing you for. Several app servers need a way to share traffic (load balancing). A database that no longer fits on one volume needs a plan to **shard** or to **replicate**. Those are not free: consistency, session stickiness, and operational complexity all appear.

A useful way to talk about the choice in an interview is: start vertical until the ceiling or the failure domain is unacceptable, then go horizontal and name the new coordination pieces.

```text
Vertical:   [ small box ]  →  [ much bigger box ]

Horizontal: [ box ] [ box ] [ box ]
                 ↑
            load balancer / shard map
```

## Common pitfalls

- Scaling up repeatedly and calling the system highly available; a large single box is still a single point of failure.
- Scaling out without a routing story, so some machines sit idle while others melt.
- Changing the data model (for example, sharding) as an afterthought once you already have uneven keys.

## Key takeaways

- Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, RAM, or disk; it is simple until you hit the limits or cost of a single box.
- Horizontal scaling adds machines and spreads work, which can add more capacity but requires distribution — routing, and often a new data layout.
- Later chapters on load balancing, health checks, and databases are the practical toolkit for going horizontal.

lessons.title: Load balancing
lessons.summary: A load balancer sits in front of several servers and spreads incoming traffic so no single instance has to take every request, and so traffic can move off a server that goes down. The lesson walks through common strategies, including round robin and other algorithms such as least connections and hash-based routing, and it ties this to fault tolerance.

quiz.question: What is the main job of a load balancer?
choices: Compile the application
Distribute incoming traffic across multiple backends
Replace the need for DNS
Convert SQL to GraphQL automatically
quiz.explanation: It spreads load and, with health information, can avoid failed instances.

quiz.question: Which of these is a common load-balancing algorithm mentioned in this kind of course?
choices: Round robin
Quicksort
MIME sniffing
CSS cascade
quiz.explanation: Round robin is a standard first example; other strategies include least connections and hash-based routing.

exercise.prompt: Name two load-balancing algorithms and one reason you might pick each. Then note what should happen if one of three app servers crashes.
exercise.hint: Round robin is simple when servers are alike. Least connections helps if some requests last longer. A crashed server should be taken out of rotation.

lessons.content:
## One entry point, many backends

A **load balancer** sits in front of several servers and **distributes incoming traffic** across those backends. No single instance has to take every request, and when a server goes down, traffic can move to the ones that are still up. That is both a capacity tool and a fault-tolerance tool.

This is the natural next drawing after horizontal scaling: you no longer send every client to one IP for one app process.

```text
Clients  →  load balancer  →  app server A
                           →  app server B
                           →  app server C
```

## Algorithms you should be able to name

Hayk walks through common strategies. The names matter in interviews because they signal *why* you chose one.

- **Round robin** — send each new request to the next server in a rotating list. It is the usual example, and it works well when servers are similar and requests are roughly even.
- **Least connections** — send the request to the server that currently has the fewest open connections. Better when some requests last much longer than others.
- **Hash-based routing** — hash something about the client (often the IP) and map it to a server, so the same client tends to keep hitting the same backend. That helps with session affinity.

Other variants you will meet in the same family include weighting (stronger machines take more work) and geography (send the user to a nearby region). The job is the same: pick a fair, explainable rule for spreading load, and be ready to say what happens when a node disappears.

## Fault tolerance, not only speed

A load balancer that only sprays traffic evenly is incomplete. It should also stop sending work to a backend that is down — which is exactly why the next lesson is about **health checks**. Until you have those, “we have three servers” can still mean “one third of users hit a dead box.”

## Common pitfalls

- Putting a load balancer in the diagram but leaving only one server behind it.
- Using round robin when in-memory sessions require stickiness, without mentioning hashing or shared session storage.
- Forgetting that the balancer itself can fail; that is the single-point-of-failure lesson shortly after this one.

## Key takeaways

- A load balancer’s main job is to distribute incoming traffic across multiple backends.
- Round robin is the common starting algorithm; least connections and hash-based routing cover uneven work and session affinity.
- Load balancing supports both scale-out and fault tolerance, especially once health checks are in place.

lessons.title: Health checks
lessons.summary: After introducing load-balancer types (including software load balancers), the lesson explains health checks: how a balancer or orchestrator tells whether an instance is fit to receive traffic. A failed check should remove or avoid that instance until it recovers. Checks can be as simple as a port or an HTTP endpoint that also verifies critical dependencies. Poorly designed checks either send users to broken nodes or flap healthy ones out of the pool.

quiz.question: What should a load balancer typically do when a backend fails its health check?
choices: Send it twice as much traffic to help it recover
Stop sending it new traffic until it looks healthy again
Delete the user’s database
Disable DNS for the whole site permanently
quiz.explanation: That is the point of a health check: keep user requests away from an unhealthy instance.

quiz.question: Why can a too-shallow health check be a problem?
choices: It may report a process as up even when a critical dependency is down
It always makes TCP faster
It replaces the need for logging
It forces you to use UDP
quiz.explanation: If the check only asks whether the process is listening, a server that cannot reach its database may still receive traffic.

exercise.prompt: Design a simple /health endpoint for a web API that uses a database. What would it check, and what status code would you return if the database is unreachable?
exercise.hint: Check that the process is up and that a cheap database ping works. Return a non-2xx status (often 503) if the dependency is down.

lessons.content:
## Watching the backends

After you put a load balancer in front of several servers, you still need to know which of those servers is fit to receive traffic. A **health check** is a repeated test the balancer (or an orchestrator) runs against each instance. When a check fails, the balancer **stops sending new traffic** to that instance until the instance looks healthy again.

Hayk first places this idea in the products you actually deploy.

## Software, hardware, and cloud balancers

**Software load balancers** are programs you install and configure yourself:

- **Nginx** is probably the most common example. It is also a web server, but it can load-balance a list of backends, apply an algorithm, and run health checks so a down server is taken out of rotation.
- **HAProxy** is an open-source alternative you likewise install on a machine and configure.

**Hardware load balancers** are dedicated appliances. Two names from the lesson are **F5** (widely used, high performance, large feature set) and **Citrix**.

If you would rather not run either of those yourself, **cloud load balancers** are the easier path. Examples:

- **AWS Elastic Load Balancing**, which can bring security features, **automatic scaling** (adding servers to the pool as demand grows), and monitoring — the cloud equivalent of health checks — without you wiring every probe by hand.
- **Azure Load Balancer** and **Google Cloud Load Balancing**, which play a similar role in those clouds.

## What a good check actually tests

A check can be as shallow as “is this port open?” That is better than nothing, but it can still report a process as up when a **critical dependency** — the database, a required cache, a downstream API — is down. In that situation users are sent to a box that cannot complete real work.

A more useful check is often an HTTP endpoint that verifies those dependencies as well as the process itself. The other failure mode is a check that is too tight or flaky, so healthy instances keep **flapping** in and out of the pool. The design job is to fail *unsafe* instances out quickly without punishing normal, brief delays.

```text
Load balancer  --periodic check-->  /health on each server
                 fail  →  leave the pool
                 pass  →  keep receiving traffic
```

## Common pitfalls

- Configuring a balancer with no health checks, so a third of users still hit a dead instance.
- Checking only that a port is listening, while the app cannot reach its database.
- Health checks so aggressive that a brief garbage-collection pause takes a good server out of rotation.

## Key takeaways

- When a backend fails its health check, the balancer should stop sending it new traffic until it recovers.
- Nginx and HAProxy are common software balancers; F5 and Citrix are hardware examples; AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud offer managed ones (AWS ELB is called out for security, autoscaling, and monitoring).
- A too-shallow check may report a process as up even when a critical dependency is down.

lessons.title: Single point of failure
lessons.summary: The obvious downside of a component you have only one of is reliability: a single failure can take the system down. A lone app server is an example; a lone load balancer, a single database primary without failover, or a single availability zone can also be single points of failure. The chapter is about spotting those bottlenecks and adding redundancy.

quiz.question: What is a single point of failure?
choices: Any component whose outage can take down the whole system
A cache that sometimes goes stale
A CSS file that failed to minify
A unit test that is skipped
quiz.explanation: If there is only one of something on the critical path, that thing is a SPOF.

quiz.question: Which of these can be a SPOF even after you add several app servers?
choices: A single load balancer that is the only entry point
Having more than one availability zone
Using a health check
Having multiple independent replicas with no shared dependency
quiz.explanation: Redundant app servers do not help if the only balancer in front of them dies.

exercise.prompt: List three potential SPOFs in a simple stack (DNS/domain, load balancer, app servers, database). For each, write one way you might reduce the risk.
exercise.hint: Examples: a managed DNS with more than one record, a pair of load balancers, several app servers, and a database with a failover replica.

lessons.content:
## The component you have only one of

A **single point of failure (SPOF)** is any component whose outage can take the whole system down. After you add several app servers and a load balancer, it is easy to feel finished — and still have a SPOF sitting in the path.

Hayk lists three reasons a SPOF is a problem, not just an inconvenience:

- **Reliability.** If the one database, or the one balancer, dies, users cannot reach the product — including high-value paths such as checkout — which means business loss.
- **Scalability.** A design full of unique, irreplaceable pieces struggles to grow, because every new unique piece is another place the whole system can fail.
- **Security.** Attackers can aim a flood of traffic at the one entry point (for example the lone load balancer). If that box fails, everything behind it is unreachable.

```text
Clients  →  [ one load balancer ]  →  many app servers
                 ↑
         if this dies, nobody gets in
```

A lone app server is the obvious SPOF. A lone load balancer, a single database primary with no failover, or a single availability zone can be one too — even after you have several app instances.

## Making the load balancer not a SPOF

Hayk postpones a full database treatment, and focuses here on the balancer you just added.

**Redundancy** is the first strategy: run **more than one** load balancer. If the second goes down, redirect all traffic to the first. When the failed balancer is healthy again, share traffic (the example in the lesson returns to a 50/50 split). Users who cannot reach one balancer can still reach the other.

The second strategy is to **health-check the load balancers themselves**, just as they health-check the app servers. Watch them continuously, and stop using one that is offline.

Avoiding a database SPOF is called out as a later (databases) concern: typically replication and failover, not a second copy of this same drawing.

## Common pitfalls

- Adding many app servers but leaving a single load balancer as the only entry point.
- Forgetting DNS, a single zone, or a single primary database when you hunt for SPOFs.
- Buying a bigger balancer instead of a pair, and calling the system highly available.

## Key takeaways

- A SPOF is any component whose outage can take down the whole system.
- Downsides include reliability (and business loss), harder scaling, and a clear target for attackers.
- A single load balancer can still be a SPOF after you add several app servers; use a redundant pair and health-check the balancers themselves.

lessons.title: API design
lessons.summary: This longer section teaches fundamental principles of API design so you can create efficient, scalable, maintainable interfaces. Hayk covers what APIs are for, the three commonly used styles REST, GraphQL, and gRPC, essential design principles, how application protocols influence those decisions, and the path from design through development to deployment.

quiz.question: Which three API styles does this course section highlight as commonly used?
choices: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC
FTP, SMTP, and POP3 only
HTML, CSS, and SVG
CSV, XML, and YAML only
quiz.explanation: Those three are the usual modern comparison set for service APIs in this course.

quiz.question: Why does API design matter in system design, not just in coding?
choices: Because the API is the contract other clients and services depend on as the system scales
Because APIs replace the need for a database
Because an API cannot fail
Because DNS cannot work without GraphQL
quiz.explanation: A poorly designed contract is hard to change later and becomes a bottleneck between teams and services.

exercise.prompt: Write a one-paragraph API design brief for a 'tasks' service: who the clients are, the main operations, and whether you would start with REST, GraphQL, or gRPC and why.
exercise.hint: A simple CRUD service for a web and mobile client often starts with REST. GraphQL can help when clients need flexible shapes. gRPC is a common choice for internal service-to-service calls.

lessons.content:
## APIs are contracts, not just endpoints

This longer section is about **API design**: how to create efficient, scalable, and maintainable interfaces between software systems.

An **API** (application programming interface) defines how software components interact. On one side is a client (a browser or a phone). On the other is a server. The API is the **contract** between them: which requests can be made, which endpoints and methods exist, and which responses to expect.

Two roles fall out of that contract:

- **Abstraction.** Callers can “save a user” without knowing how the server stores that user. Implementation stays hidden; the interface is what they depend on.
- **Service boundaries.** Clear interfaces let you split work across servers — one service for users, another for posts — and let different systems talk even when their internals differ.

Because other clients and services depend on that contract as the system scales, API design is a system-design problem, not only a coding style.

## Three common styles: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC

Hayk highlights three styles you will see throughout the rest of the course.

**REST** (Representational State Transfer) is the most common, especially for web and mobile apps. It is organized around resources and standard HTTP methods. A key property is that REST APIs are **stateless**: each request carries everything needed to process it.

**GraphQL** is the second most common. It is a query language that lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs. A practical benefit is **fewer round trips**: data that would have taken several REST calls can often be fetched in one query.

**gRPC** (gRPC Remote Procedure Calls) is the least common of the three in public web APIs, but it is important inside service meshes. It is a high-performance RPC framework. Services are defined in **Protocol Buffer** (`.proto`) files, and it supports **streaming** and bidirectional communication. It is a strong fit for service-to-service calls where you control both ends.

## Four design principles

Hayk’s test for a great API is blunt: *the best API is the one you can use without reading the documentation.* A `GET /users/123` that silently also updates followers fails that test. The four pillars are:

1. **Consistency** — same naming, casing, and patterns everywhere. Mixing camelCase `userDetails` in one place with snake_case `user/details` in another is a consistency bug.
2. **Simplicity** — focus on core use cases and an intuitive shape. Minimize complexity so developers understand the API quickly.
3. **Security** — authentication and authorization, input validation, and rate limiting as a baseline.
4. **Performance** — caching, **pagination** (limit and offset, so “get posts” does not return thousands of rows), smaller payloads, and fewer round trips when related data can travel with the main response.

## Protocols shape the design

Your protocol choice changes what the API can do. HTTP naturally supports REST (methods, status codes, CRUD-style operations). **WebSockets** enable bidirectional, real-time APIs such as chat or streaming. GraphQL typically still rides on HTTP. gRPC is often used between microservices for speed, rather than as the browser-facing protocol. Choose based on those strengths and limits; the next lesson goes deeper on the protocols themselves.

## The design process

Work starts with **requirements**: core use cases and user stories, a clear scope (and what is out of scope), performance bottlenecks, and security constraints (authn, authz, rate limits, and anything extra the product needs).

Three design approaches appear:

- **Top-down** — start from high-level requirements and workflows, then name endpoints. Common in interviews.
- **Bottom-up** — start from existing data models and capabilities, which is common inside a company that already has both.
- **Contract-first** — write the request and response contract before implementation. Close to top-down, and also common in interviews.

The lifecycle is design, then development and local testing, then deploy and monitor (staging or production), then **maintenance** (another reason to keep the API simple), and eventually **deprecation**. Versioning (for example `/v1`, then `/v2`, or field-level versioning) is how you change a contract without surprising existing clients.

## Common pitfalls

- Treating the API as “just the controllers,” and changing response shapes without a versioning plan.
- Inconsistent naming, or GET endpoints that have surprising side effects.
- Skipping pagination and shipping entire collections.
- Choosing gRPC for a public browser client that cannot speak HTTP/2 comfortably.

## Key takeaways

- An API is the contract other clients and services depend on as the system scales.
- The three styles this section highlights are REST, GraphQL, and gRPC.
- Great APIs are consistent, simple, secure, and performant — ideally usable without reading docs.
- Protocol choice, requirements, top-down vs bottom-up vs contract-first design, and a lifecycle through deprecation all belong in the design conversation.

lessons.title: API protocols
lessons.summary: Choosing the wrong application protocol can lead to performance bottlenecks. HTTP is the default for many REST and GraphQL APIs; other choices such as gRPC over HTTP/2 change how you version, stream, and handle errors. The lesson ties protocol choice to the API style and to the needs of the clients.

quiz.question: Why does the application protocol matter when you design an API?
choices: It decides how clients and servers exchange requests, errors, and (sometimes) streams
It selects the database engine automatically
It is only a documentation theme
It replaces authentication
quiz.explanation: HTTP, HTTP/2 plus gRPC, and other protocols have different constraints and strengths.

quiz.question: What protocol is the usual transport for a public REST or GraphQL HTTP API?
choices: HTTP (often with TLS, as HTTPS)
SMTP only
FTP only
IMAP only
quiz.explanation: REST and browser-facing GraphQL APIs are typically served over HTTPS.

exercise.prompt: For a public JSON API used by a website, and for a high-throughput internal service-to-service API, say which protocol style you would prefer and why.
exercise.hint: Public web clients almost always use HTTPS JSON/REST or GraphQL. Internal services often use gRPC or HTTP, depending on tooling and streaming needs.

lessons.content:
## Why the protocol is part of the design

Choosing the wrong application protocol can create performance bottlenecks and cut off features you need. Hayk treats protocol choice as a design decision: match it to latency, throughput, and interaction patterns.

Application-layer protocols sit at the top of the network stack, on top of transport protocols such as TCP and UDP (the next lesson). They define message formats, request/response patterns, connections, and error handling. For API work, the protocols you actually pick among are HTTP, HTTPS, WebSockets, AMQP, and gRPC.

## HTTP and HTTPS

**HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of most web APIs. A client sends a request that includes a **method**, a resource URL (for example `/api/products/…`), the HTTP version, a host, and often credentials (a bearer token, basic auth, OAuth, and so on). The server replies with a status code, a content type (often `application/json`), and a body.

Methods in this lesson: **GET** to retrieve, **POST** to create, **PUT** or **PATCH** to update (full or partial), **DELETE** to remove.

Status-code families:

- 2xx — success (for example 200)
- 3xx — redirection
- 4xx — the client made an error
- 5xx — the server failed

Common headers include `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Accept`, `Cache-Control`, and `User-Agent`.

**HTTPS** is HTTP with **TLS/SSL** encryption. Data is protected in transit, with integrity and a certificate-based security layer. Hayk also notes SEO benefits and is blunt about the alternative: using plain HTTP is risky; HTTPS is the default you should use on servers.

## WebSockets for real time

HTTP is a request/response model. For a chat app, polling (“any new messages?”) on a timer produces empty responses, extra latency, wasted bandwidth, and wasted server work.

**WebSockets** start with a handshake and then keep a **bidirectional** connection. The server can *push* new messages as soon as they exist, and the client can still send when it needs to. That is what makes real-time updates practical: lower latency and no empty poll cycles.

## AMQP and gRPC

**AMQP** (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) is an enterprise messaging protocol used for **asynchronous** work and guaranteed delivery. A **producer** (a web service or payment system) publishes to a **broker** with queues (for example an order-processing queue). A **consumer** (a payment processor or notification service) pulls a message when it has capacity, and leaves it queued when it is busy. Exchange types mentioned here — direct, fan-out, and topic — are flagged for a later message-queuing section.

**gRPC** is a high-performance RPC framework from Google. It uses **Protocol Buffers** and **HTTP/2** for transport, and therefore has built-in streaming. Clients must support HTTP/2, which is why gRPC is most often used **between servers** (microservices), not from typical browsers.

## How to choose

| Need | Lean toward |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary request/response from a web or mobile client | HTTP/HTTPS (the default) |
| Real-time chat or live updates | WebSockets |
| Async work between a producer and a consumer | AMQP and a queue |
| Fast service-to-service calls you control | gRPC over HTTP/2 |

Also weigh payload size and encoding, security (authentication and encryption), client compatibility, and developer experience (tooling and documentation). A public REST or GraphQL API almost always sits on HTTP, usually as HTTPS.

## Common pitfalls

- Polling over HTTP for a truly real-time product, then wondering why the chat feels laggy.
- Exposing gRPC directly to browsers that do not speak HTTP/2 well.
- Shipping a public API on plain HTTP.
- Using a queue when the caller needed a synchronous answer in the same request.

## Key takeaways

- The application protocol decides how clients and servers exchange requests, errors, and sometimes streams.
- HTTP (typically HTTPS, with TLS) is the usual transport for a public REST or GraphQL API.
- WebSockets unlock server push; AMQP supports asynchronous queued work; gRPC over HTTP/2 is a high-performance choice between services.
- Pick the protocol for the interaction pattern, performance, and what the client can actually speak.

lessons.title: Transport layer: TCP and UDP
lessons.summary: Most developers work with APIs without thinking about what is actually delivering the bytes. Under the application protocol is the transport. TCP is connection-oriented and aims to deliver a reliable, ordered stream — a good default for payments or most APIs. UDP is lighter and does not guarantee delivery or order, which can be the right trade-off for latency-sensitive media where a late packet is useless.

quiz.question: Which statement about TCP versus UDP is accurate?
choices: TCP is connection-oriented and aims to deliver data reliably and in order; UDP is lighter and does not guarantee delivery or order
UDP always retries more than TCP, so it is slower for every use case
TCP cannot be used for HTTP
UDP assigns IP addresses
quiz.explanation: That trade-off is why APIs and payments usually sit on TCP, while some real-time media uses UDP.

quiz.question: Which traffic is a better default for UDP than for TCP?
choices: A bank transfer API that must not lose a request
A live video stream where a late packet is better dropped than retried
Storing a user’s password hash
A database migration
quiz.explanation: Retransmitting an old video frame can hurt more than skipping it.

exercise.prompt: Choose TCP or UDP for: a checkout API, a DNS query (as typically designed), and a real-time game position update. Give a one-line reason for each.
exercise.hint: Checkout: TCP. Classic DNS: often UDP. Game state: often UDP, with the app handling loss.

lessons.content:
## Under the application protocol

Most developers work with APIs without thinking about what is actually delivering the bytes. Under HTTP, WebSockets, or gRPC is the **transport layer**. The two protocols Hayk compares are **TCP** and **UDP**. They both move data from one machine to another, but they do it very differently.

(He refers to this as a lower layer in the OSI model — the important idea is that it sits *under* the application protocols from the previous lesson.)

## TCP: reliable and connection-oriented

**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) is the reliable-but-heavier option. Think of sending a parcel with a receipt, tracking, and a signature.

Data is often split into chunks. TCP’s job is to **deliver all of them**, **in order**. If a packet is lost or arrives out of sequence, TCP resends or reorders it. Before any of that, it is **connection-based**: client and server perform a **three-way handshake** (the client requests, the server syncs and acknowledges, the client acknowledges) and only then exchange data.

That bookkeeping is overhead, and it makes TCP slower than UDP, but it is accurate. APIs that involve **payments, authentication, or user data** — banking, email, and similar — should use TCP. If a packet is lost, TCP waits and resends rather than silently dropping the data.

## UDP: lighter, with no delivery guarantee

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is faster and has less overhead because it does **not** guarantee delivery, order, a handshake, or connection tracking. If one of four packets never arrives, UDP will not make sure it eventually shows up.

That is a feature when a late packet is useless. On a **video call**, a **live stream**, or an **online game**, you would rather skip the laggy fragment and continue with the next one than pause to retransmit old audio. Hayk’s rule of thumb: choose UDP when you need speed and some loss is acceptable; choose TCP when you need the connection to be safe and complete.

|  | TCP | UDP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection | Yes — three-way handshake | No handshake |
| Delivery | Aims to deliver everything, in order, with retries | No guarantee of delivery or order |
| Overhead | Higher | Lower, faster |
| Typical use | Payments, auth, email, most APIs | Live video, calls, games, streams |

```text
TCP handshake (simplified):
  Client  -- SYN -->  Server
  Client  <-- SYN-ACK --  Server
  Client  -- ACK -->  Server
  (connection is up; data can flow)
```

## Common pitfalls

- Using UDP for a payment or login API because “it’s faster.”
- Using TCP for a live video stream and then fighting delay caused by retransmission of stale frames.
- Confusing the transport (TCP/UDP) with the application protocol (HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC).

## Key takeaways

- TCP is connection-oriented and aims to deliver data reliably and in order; UDP is lighter and does not guarantee delivery or order.
- Use TCP for banking, payments, authentication, and most APIs.
- Use UDP when a late packet should be dropped — live video, calls, games, and similar streams.
- For building APIs, the layers you actually choose among are the application protocols plus this transport choice.

lessons.title: RESTful APIs
lessons.summary: RESTful APIs let different parts of a system talk to each other using standard HTTP. The design models the API around resources (nouns) and uses methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. URLs are typically hierarchical, query parameters handle filtering, sorting, and pagination, and status codes communicate success and error classes so the API stays predictable for clients.

quiz.question: In a RESTful design, what should a URL usually represent?
choices: A verb such as /getUser
A resource (a noun), such as /users/42
A raw SQL query
An IP address only
quiz.explanation: Operations then come from the HTTP method, not from packing verbs into the path.

quiz.question: Why do list endpoints often support pagination?
choices: To keep responses bounded and reduce bandwidth as collections grow
Because HTTP forbids returning more than one record
Because REST cannot use JSON
Because pagination replaces authentication
quiz.explanation: Page/limit, offset, or cursor patterns all exist to avoid dumping an entire table.

exercise.prompt: Design REST endpoints for a 'books' resource: list, get one, create, update, and delete. Add a query for paging the list, and pick status codes for a successful create and a missing book.
exercise.hint: GET /books?page=&limit=, GET /books/{id}, POST /books, PUT or PATCH /books/{id}, DELETE /books/{id}. 201 for create, 404 if the book is missing.

lessons.content:
## REST is resource-oriented HTTP

RESTful APIs let different parts of a system talk to each other using standard HTTP. They are the most common way developers build and consume APIs today. This lesson is about designing them cleanly so you do not end up with messy, inconsistent patterns that are hard to use and maintain.

The core idea is **resources**, not verbs in the URL. Start from the business domain — products, orders, reviews — and model those as **nouns**. `/api/products` is a collection; `/api/products/{id}` is one item; `/api/products/{id}/reviews` is a nested collection of reviews for that product. You do *not* invent `/getProducts` or `/delete`. The **HTTP method** says what to do; the URL says *which resource*.

```text
GET    /api/v1/products           → collection
GET    /api/v1/products/123       → one product
POST   /api/v1/products           → create in the collection
PUT    /api/v1/products/123       → replace that product
PATCH  /api/v1/products/123       → partial update
DELETE /api/v1/products/123       → remove it
```

## Filtering, sorting, and pagination

You almost never want to return an entire collection at once. Those controls usually live in **query parameters** (the part of the URL after `?`).

- **Filtering** — for example `?category=shoes&inStock=true` returns only the items the UI will show, instead of wasting bandwidth on a huge response.
- **Sorting** — for example a `sort` parameter for price or reviews, ascending or descending. Sorting belongs on the **server**. If the database has 1,000 products and the client wants them by price, do not download all 1,000 and sort in the browser.
- **Pagination** — common shapes are `page` plus `limit`; **offset** plus `limit` (start counting from this index); or a **cursor** (a token/hash for the next page). Without a limit, you are back to shipping the whole collection.

The payoff is less bandwidth, better performance on both sides, and more flexibility for the client, which can ask only for what the current view needs. List endpoints should stay bounded as collections grow.

## Methods, safety, and status codes

REST leans on HTTP for CRUD:

| Method | Typical job | Notes from the lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | Read a collection or an item | Safe and **idempotent**: repeating the request should not change server state (the catalog can still grow for other reasons) |
| POST | Create a resource, usually on the collection URL | Changes state; **not** idempotent — two POSTs create two items with two IDs |
| PUT | Replace the whole resource at that ID | Same URL as PATCH; the body is the new complete representation |
| PATCH | Update only the fields you send | For example, change a title and leave the rest alone |
| DELETE | Remove the resource | Same item URL; typically no body |

Use status codes that match the outcome:

- **2xx success** — `200 OK` for a successful read, `201 Created` after a POST that created a resource (not another 200), `204 No Content` when there is nothing to return.
- **3xx redirection** — the resource has moved; follow the new URL.
- **4xx client errors** — `400 Bad Request` for invalid parameters or broken JSON; `401` when the caller is not authenticated; `404 Not Found` when the product ID does not exist.
- **5xx server errors** — the request looked fine, but the server failed unexpectedly; typically `500` with a server error message.

## Best practices

- Use **plural nouns**: `/products`, not `/product`.
- Use the proper method and a resource URL; do not invent `/users/42/delete` or a POST to “delete.”
- Support filtering, sorting, and pagination together — a `page` without a `limit` is still a blunt tool.
- **Version** the API, often as a prefix such as `/api/v1`, then `/api/v2`. When you add breaking changes, existing clients can stay on v1 while you develop v3.

Together, those habits keep the API consistent and predictable for other developers.

## Common pitfalls

- Verbs in the path (`/getOrders`) instead of a noun plus a method.
- Returning an entire unfiltered, unsorted, unpaginated list.
- Answering a successful POST with 200 instead of 201.
- Shipping a breaking change on the same URL with no version.

## Key takeaways

- In a RESTful design, a URL usually represents a resource (a noun), such as `/users/42` or `/api/v1/products/123`.
- GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE map onto read, create, replace, partial update, and delete; GET is idempotent, POST is not.
- Query parameters handle filtering, sorting, and pagination (page/limit, offset/limit, or cursor) so responses stay bounded.
- Status codes communicate success and error classes; versioning keeps old clients working when the contract changes.

lessons.title: GraphQL
lessons.summary: Traditional RESTful APIs often return too much or too little data, which is the problem GraphQL is introduced to solve. Clients can ask for exactly the fields they need, often in one request, instead of stitching several REST endpoints. The trade-offs include a more complex server, caching that is less natural than plain HTTP GET, and the need to protect against expensive queries.

quiz.question: What problem with traditional REST APIs does this lesson use to introduce GraphQL?
choices: They often return too much or too little data for a given client
They cannot use HTTPS
They cannot return JSON
They only work on FTP
quiz.explanation: The transcript contrasts REST payloads that over-fetch or under-fetch with GraphQL’s ability to request a specific shape.

quiz.question: What is a common trade-off of GraphQL compared with simple REST GET endpoints?
choices: HTTP caching and cost control can be harder, and the server has to police expensive queries
It cannot return JSON
It only works on FTP
It removes the need for any schema
quiz.explanation: A single GraphQL endpoint and nested queries change how you cache and how you limit work.

exercise.prompt: Write a small GraphQL-style query for a user and that user’s last three orders (fields: id, name, order id and total). Then note one risk you would guard against on the server.
exercise.hint: A query like user { id name orders(last: 3) { id total } }. Guard against deeply nested or unbounded list queries.

lessons.content:
## Why GraphQL exists

Traditional REST APIs often return **too much or too little** data. A single screen may need a user, their posts, comments, and likes, which in a REST design can mean several endpoints and still the wrong shape. Facebook created GraphQL to fix that pain: clients were making multiple calls and still not getting exactly what the view needed, which added latency while the page waited.

In GraphQL the client talks to **one endpoint** and **specifies the shape of the response**. It is still HTTP, but a request can ask for user `123`, only `name`, and from `posts` only `title` — no images, no unused fields. That avoids **over-fetching**. One query can replace several REST round trips.

```text
query {
  user(id: "123") {
    name
    posts { title }
  }
}
```

## Schema, types, queries, and mutations

The **schema** is the contract between client and server. You define **types** that should mirror the domain and stay intuitive. A `User` type might have `id`, `name`, and `posts`; `posts` is not a primitive, so you define a `Post` type and say the field is a list of posts.

**Queries** are the read side — the equivalent of GET in REST. You declare a query field such as `user(id:)` that returns a `User`.

**Mutations** are the write side — the equivalent of POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Anytime you change data, you run a mutation. A `createUser` mutation might accept a name (and, in a real API, more fields) and return the `User` type. When mutating, a best practice in the lesson is to use **input types** rather than a loose list of arguments. A `createPost` mutation can set `title` and `body`, and the client still says which fields it wants back (`id`, `title`).

## Errors are not ordinary HTTP status codes

Error handling differs from REST. GraphQL typically returns **HTTP 200 OK even when something failed**. The failure is described in an `errors` field on the body. **Partial data** can still be returned alongside those errors — for example `user` is `null`, and `errors` lists a status such as 404, a “not found” message, and the `path` (`user`). Because the HTTP status is always 200, that embedded status (or a similar code in the error object) is how the client learns *what kind* of error it was.

## Design practices and trade-offs

Best practices from the lesson:

- Keep schemas **small and modular**.
- Avoid infinitely nested queries (`user → posts → comments → …`). Set a **query depth limit** (Hayk’s example is about six or seven layers).
- Use **meaningful names** for types and fields; clients and servers share the same schema.
- Use **input types** for mutations.

Compared with simple REST GET endpoints, HTTP caching is less natural (almost everything is a POST to one URL), and the server must **police expensive queries**. Depth limits are one way to do that. GraphQL shines when many clients need different slices of the same graph; it is not automatically simpler to operate.

## Common pitfalls

- Rebuilding six REST endpoints as one GraphQL API, then allowing unbounded nested queries that take the database down.
- Treating HTTP 200 as “the user was found”; always read the `errors` array.
- Over-fetching again by asking for every field “just in case,” which throws away GraphQL’s main benefit.

## Key takeaways

- GraphQL exists because REST often returns too much or too little data, forcing extra round trips.
- Clients ask one endpoint for exactly the fields they need; queries read, mutations write, and the schema is the contract.
- Responses are usually HTTP 200; failures belong in an `errors` field, sometimes with partial data.
- Limit query depth, keep schemas modular, and remember that caching and cost control are harder than with plain REST GETs.

lessons.title: Authentication
lessons.summary: Before a system can authorize or restrict anything, it first needs to know who the caller is. This long chapter surveys common methods: basic and digest auth, API keys, session cookies, JWTs (often with access and refresh tokens), and sign-in frameworks such as OAuth2, OpenID Connect, and SAML that also enable single sign-on. The right choice depends on whether you are authenticating a user, a machine, or a third-party app.

quiz.question: What is authentication, as opposed to authorization?
choices: Verifying who the caller is
Deciding which resources that caller may access
Encrypting a hard drive at rest
Balancing traffic across servers
quiz.explanation: Authentication establishes identity. Authorization decides what that identity is allowed to do.

quiz.question: Which of these is a typical use of OAuth2 or OpenID Connect?
choices: Letting a user sign in (or grant a third-party app access) without sharing their password with every service
Choosing between SQL and NoSQL
Compressing images at the CDN
Sorting an array in linear time
quiz.explanation: Those protocols are widely used for delegated access and for single sign-on experiences.

exercise.prompt: For a public HTTP API used by a first-party mobile app, pick an authentication approach (for example session cookies, API keys, or JWT access/refresh tokens) and list one advantage and one risk you would have to handle.
exercise.hint: Mobile apps often use access and refresh tokens. Risks include token theft, refresh-token rotation, and storing secrets on the device.

lessons.content:
## Authentication answers “who is this?”

Before a system can authorize or restrict anything, it needs to know **who the caller is** — a person in a browser or app, or a third-party service. **Authentication** verifies that claim. A typical picture is an API gateway in front of services and storage: the client sends a login (or a credential on the request); if identity is confirmed they may proceed, otherwise the gateway responds **401 Unauthorized**. What they are *allowed to do* after that is authorization, and it is a separate lesson.

Hayk spends time untangling vocabulary people mix up:

- **JWT** is a **token format**, not an authentication method by itself.
- **Bearer** is a *pattern* (“whoever holds this token is allowed through”), not a synonym for JWT — though JWT is the most common bearer token.
- **OAuth 2** is an **authorization framework**, not an authentication method.
- **Single sign-on** is a **user-experience pattern** (log in once, use many services), not a method of its own.

## Basic, digest, API keys, and sessions

**Basic authentication** is the simplest flow. A request without credentials gets 401; the next request sends an `Authorization` header with a **Base64** encoding of `username:password`. If that checks out, the server returns 200 and the data. The problem is that Base64 is easily reversed, so this is insecure unless it is wrapped in **HTTPS** — and even then it is rare in production outside internal tools, because the password travels on every request.

**Digest authentication** is slightly better: it uses **MD5 hashing** instead of sending the password in reversible form. The overall dance is similar to basic auth. It is still considered outdated compared with the later methods in this lesson.

**API keys** are unique secrets you generate for a client. The client sends the key; the server looks it up in a permissions or users table. If it is missing, you might return 400 because the key is required. Issues: if the key leaks, anyone can act as that client; there is **no built-in expiration** unless you add one; and a key is just a random string with **no embedded information**. A JWT, by contrast, can carry claims. Tools such as Postman may list API keys next to “authentication frameworks,” which adds to the naming confusion.

**Session-based authentication** is the traditional web approach. The user logs in; the server creates a session in **session storage** and sets a **session cookie**. Later requests present the cookie; the server looks up the session and either returns the user or 401. Storage options: in-memory (lost on restart), **Redis** (the usual production choice — fast, with built-in expiration), a SQL database, or (rarely) the filesystem, which does not scale well. The challenge is that sessions are **stateful**: the server must remember them. That works for traditional web apps and is harder to scale for APIs and distributed systems.

## Bearer tokens, JWTs, access and refresh

Modern apps often send a **token** on each request, commonly as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A **JWT** (JSON Web Token) is a **signed JSON object** that can hold a user id or email, an expiration, and other **claims** such as roles. After the first credential check, the server issues the JWT; later requests can be **verified by signature locally**, without a database lookup. That is why JWTs are described as **stateless** and more scalable than sessions. (Older opaque tokens still needed a database or cache on every use.)

Systems often issue **two** tokens:

- An **access token**, short-lived (Hayk’s range is about **15 minutes to 1 hour**), used for API calls.
- A **refresh token**, long-lived (**days or weeks**), used only to mint a new access token when the old one expires.

Store the refresh token in an **HTTP-only cookie**, not in `localStorage`, to reduce **XSS** risk. When an expired access token yields 401, the client uses the refresh token at the auth server, then retries the API call. The user stays signed in without typing the password again.

## OAuth 2, OpenID Connect, SSO, and SAML

**OAuth 2** answers *what can this app access on the user’s behalf?* Example: you connect an app to **Google Drive** so it can read files. You see a **consent** screen; if you allow it, the app receives an **authorization code**, exchanges the code for an **access token**, and calls the Drive API. That token proves the *app* may access certain resources. It does **not** by itself tell the app *who you are*.

**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** adds **authentication on top of OAuth 2**. “Sign in with Google” (or GitHub, Microsoft, and similar) redirects you to the provider; after consent you exchange a code for an **access token plus an ID token**. The ID token is a JWT with identity (email, username, user id). Your app verifies the signature, learns who the user is, and can create its own session. This is the modern, scalable pattern behind many “Sign in with …” buttons.

**Single sign-on (SSO)** is the experience of logging in **once** and reaching several services — Gmail, Drive, YouTube, Calendar — through an **identity provider** such as Google or Okta. A global session and an SSO cookie mean the second service does not ask you to log in again. Under the hood, SSO uses **identity protocols**:

- **SAML** (Security Assertion Markup Language) — XML-based, common in **enterprise and legacy** settings (Salesforce, corporate dashboards). After login you get a SAML assertion in XML.
- **OpenID Connect** — the more modern option; you get an ID token as a JWT. Google uses this style under the hood. Both can be secure and remain in use.

## Common pitfalls

- Calling JWT or OAuth 2 “an authentication method” and stopping there; know which layer each name belongs to.
- Sending basic-auth passwords without HTTPS, or using basic auth on a public API.
- Putting refresh tokens in `localStorage`, where XSS can steal them.
- Treating an OAuth access token as proof of identity when you never received an ID token.

## Key takeaways

- Authentication verifies who the caller is; a failed check is typically 401.
- Methods include basic and digest auth, API keys, session cookies, and bearer JWTs, often with short-lived access tokens and longer-lived refresh tokens.
- JWT is a signed, self-contained token format; bearer is the “hold the token” pattern.
- OAuth 2 delegates *authorization* to an app; OpenID Connect adds an ID token so you can sign the user in; SSO is the login-once experience, usually via SAML or OIDC.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.summary: Authentication is only the first step before users can access a service. Authorization decides what an already-identified caller is allowed to do, using roles, permissions, or attribute-based rules. A secure API checks authorization on every sensitive operation, not only at the login screen, and defaults to denying access when a rule is missing.

quiz.question: What does authorization decide?
choices: Which actions and resources an already-identified caller is allowed to use
The caller’s display name only
Which load-balancing algorithm to enable
Whether TCP or UDP is used
quiz.explanation: It is the 'what can you do?' step after authentication.

quiz.question: Why is it not enough to authorize only at login?
choices: Each request or action can require a different permission, and tokens or sessions can be reused
Because login never authenticates the user
Because authorization is handled only by DNS
Because APIs cannot send cookies
quiz.explanation: A logged-in user still must not be able to edit someone else’s order just because they have a valid session.

exercise.prompt: Define two roles for a blog API, such as author and admin. List which endpoints each role may call, and say what an unauthenticated caller may read.
exercise.hint: Public readers might GET published posts. Authors can create and edit their own. Admins can moderate or delete any post.

lessons.content:
## After “who,” decide “what”

Authentication is only the first step. It tells you **who** the caller is. **Authorization** decides **which actions and resources** that already-identified caller may use, and which are denied. That is how applications control security and privacy. Checking only at login is not enough: each later request can need a different permission, and a token or session can be reused.

Hayk’s running example is **GitHub** repositories. User A might have **write** access (can push). User B might have **read** only (cannot push or open pull requests). An **admin** might have full control, including settings and even deleting the repo. Same system, different authorization.

## Three authorization models

**Role-based access control (RBAC)** assigns users to **roles**, and each role has a set of permissions. Typical roles: **admin** (create, read, update, delete, and manage other users), **editor** (create, read, and update, but not delete or manage users), **viewer** (read only). This is the most common model, and you will see it in GitHub, **Stripe** dashboards, CMS tools, and team-management products.

**Attribute-based access control (ABAC)** goes beyond roles. Policies combine **user attributes** (department, age), **resource attributes** (confidentiality, owner, classification), and **environment** conditions (time of day, location, device). Example: allow access only if the user’s department is HR *and* the resource is marked internal. ABAC is more flexible than RBAC and can be combined with it, but it needs careful policy management and can produce conflicting rules.

**Access control lists (ACLs)** attach a **permission list to a resource**. For a document, Alice might have read, Bob read and write, and someone else no access. ACLs are highly specific and user-centric. They are harder to scale to millions of users or objects unless you manage them carefully — but it is possible: **Google Drive / Google Docs** is the lesson’s example, where you share one document with a colleague as a viewer and another as an editor. You get fine-grained control per file; the trade-off is operational scale.

Real systems often **combine** models. There is no single always-right choice; it depends on the product.

| Model | How permission is decided | Strength | Watch-out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RBAC | User → role → permissions | Simple, familiar | Coarse if every exception becomes a new role |
| ABAC | Attributes of user, resource, and environment | Very flexible | Policy complexity and conflicts |
| ACL | Per-resource list of users and verbs | Precise sharing, as in Docs | Harder to scale naively |

## Enforcing the rules: OAuth 2 and tokens

Models describe *what is allowed*. **Tokens** are a common *mechanism* for carrying identity and claims on each request.

**OAuth 2** is **delegated authorization**: a service accesses another service’s resources on the user’s behalf, **without taking the user’s password**. Example: deploying on **Vercel**, you grant Vercel access to a **GitHub** repository. GitHub issues a token that represents the permissions you approved (read these repos, maybe push, but not delete). The third-party app uses that token, not your GitHub password.

**JWT or bearer tokens** often travel on later API calls and can carry a user id, roles (admin, editor), **scopes**, expiry, and issuer. The server validates the token and then applies permission logic. Important distinction: the token carries **identity and claims**; RBAC, ABAC, and ACLs are what **define** what those claims are allowed to do. Do not confuse the mechanism with the model.

A secure API checks authorization on **every sensitive operation** and should **default to deny** when a rule is missing.

## Common pitfalls

- Authorizing only at login, then trusting every request that still has a cookie or token.
- Giving a third-party app your password instead of a scoped OAuth token.
- Creating dozens of one-off roles instead of attributes or an ACL when the rules are about the document, not the job title.
- Treating “the JWT decoded” as “the action is allowed” without checking the role, scope, or ACL.

## Key takeaways

- Authorization decides what an already-identified caller may do; check it on each sensitive action, not only at login.
- The three models in this lesson are RBAC (roles), ABAC (attributes and conditions), and ACLs (per-resource lists), with GitHub, policy-based HR examples, and Google Docs as illustrations.
- OAuth 2 issues scoped tokens so an app can act for a user without the password; JWTs can carry roles and scopes, but they are a mechanism, not a model.
- Real systems often combine models, and each has trade-offs.

lessons.title: Security
lessons.summary: Hayk compares APIs to doors into your system: if you leave them unprotected, attackers can reach user data. He then walks through seven proven techniques for protecting APIs. The first on the list is rate limiting, which controls how many requests a client can make in a given time. The rest of the chapter gathers related production habits: TLS in transit, careful secret handling, input validation, and reducing blast radius when something goes wrong.

quiz.question: How does this lesson describe APIs when introducing security?
choices: As doors into your system that must be protected, or attackers can walk in
As a replacement for a database
As a font choice in the marketing site
As optional documentation only
quiz.explanation: Hayk’s opening metaphor is that APIs are doors; if you leave them unprotected, anyone can reach user data.

choices: Rate limiting, which controls how many requests a client can make in a given time
Choosing a warmer brand color
Disabling TLS
Deleting all logs
quiz.explanation: He says he will cover seven proven techniques and starts the list with rate limiting.

exercise.prompt: Write a short security checklist for a new public API: transport, secrets, input validation, and abuse. One bullet for each.
exercise.hint: HTTPS everywhere; secrets in a vault or env, not in git; validate and bound all input; rate-limit by IP or user.

lessons.content:
## APIs are doors into your system

Hayk compares APIs to **doors**. If you leave them unprotected, attackers can walk in and reach user data. This lesson walks through **seven proven techniques** for protecting APIs, then the course wraps (he mentions further deep dives and case studies such as WhatsApp, Spotify, and TinyURL on his channel — useful context, not part of the seven).

## 1. Rate limiting

**Rate limiting** controls how many requests a client can make in a given time. If the client is over the cap, you **block the next request** and make them wait. Without a limit, attackers can flood the API or brute-force data.

Limits can be set **per endpoint**, and also **per user IP**. In the lesson’s sketch, clients A, B, and C are ordinary users and D is an attacker; the 101st request from D’s IP is rejected. Per-IP limits are not enough on their own: an attacker can **spin up many IPs**. That is why you also want an **overall** rate limit — a higher cap on total traffic — to help absorb **DDoS**-style floods.

## 2. CORS

**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) controls **which domains may call your API from a browser**. Without it, a malicious site could trick a user’s browser into calling your API. If the API is meant only for `app.yourdomain.com`, requests from `app.anotherdomain.com` should be blocked so that other origins cannot authenticate or use your data.

## 3. Injection protection

**SQL and NoSQL injection** happens when user input is **concatenated into a database query**. An attacker can change the query to read, modify, or delete data — including wiping tables — by bypassing checks. The fix taught here is to always use **parameterized queries** or **ORM safeguards**, never to paste raw input into query strings.

## 4. Firewalls

A **firewall** sits between incoming traffic and your API and filters malicious requests from normal ones. A **web application firewall**, such as **AWS WAF**, can block known attack patterns — suspicious SQL keywords, strange HTTP methods — while letting ordinary traffic through.

## 5. VPNs for private APIs

Some APIs should not be on the public internet at all. A **VPN** (virtual private network) keeps those APIs reachable only from inside the same network. Public APIs accept internet users; **internal** APIs — for example an **admin dashboard** — should reject a request from the open web and accept only employees connected to the company VPN.

## 6. CSRF tokens

**CSRF** (cross-site request forgery) tricks a **logged-in user’s browser** into making an unwanted request. The banking example: the bank uses **session cookies**. A malicious page can cause the browser to send those cookies with a hidden “transfer money” request. The defense is a **CSRF token** in addition to the session cookie. The bank checks both; if the token does not match, the foreign request is blocked.

## 7. XSS

**XSS** (cross-site scripting) lets attackers **inject scripts into pages** served to other users. In a **comment** field, a normal comment is stored and shown; a comment that contains a script can be saved, then executed in **other users’ browsers** when they load the thread — for example to steal a cookie or attack the app further. You must treat stored content as untrusted and encode or sanitize it so the browser never runs it as JavaScript.

```text
Attacker posts <script>…</script> as a comment
        → API stores it
        → later visitors load the thread
        → their browsers run the script
```

## Common pitfalls

- Rate-limiting only per IP, and then falling over when the attacker uses many addresses.
- Reflecting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on an authenticated API.
- Building queries with string concatenation “just this once.”
- Putting an admin API on the public internet with only a secret URL.
- Relying on session cookies alone for state-changing requests, with no CSRF token.
- Rendering user HTML or comments without encoding, which is an XSS bug.

## Key takeaways

- APIs are doors into the system and must be protected, or attackers can walk in.
- The first technique on the list of seven is rate limiting (per endpoint, per IP, and an overall cap against DDoS).
- The other six are CORS, injection-safe queries (parameterized queries or an ORM), firewalls (including WAFs), VPNs for private/internal APIs, CSRF tokens with cookies, and XSS defenses on stored content.
